name: Participle clauses: Having finished…, The man sitting there…
subtitle: A participle clause packs a second idea into a short phrase: Walking home, I saw Tom. The man sitting there is my uncle. Having finished the report, she left.
source: icanspeak English original English text (grammar-c1 run, 2026-10-29)

concept.exampleHtml: Walking home, I saw Tom. — The man sitting there is my uncle. — Having finished the report, she left.

qa.html: Two jobs. A participle clause can stand before or after a main clause and give a time, a reason or a condition: Walking home, I saw Tom. (= While I was walking home…) Or it can stand after a noun and work like a relative clause: the man sitting there (= the man who is sitting there). Both are typical of written English: news, reports, stories.

Which form? -ing is active and happens at the same time: Walking home, I saw Tom. -ed (past participle) is passive, something was done to the subject: Shocked by the news, he sat down. Having + -ed shows that the action came first: Having finished the report, she left. (She finished, then she left.)

Same subject. In an adverbial participle clause, the subject of the main clause is also the subject of the participle. Walking home, I saw Tom. = I was walking. If the subject is different, the sentence is wrong (a dangling participle): ✗ Walking home, the rain started. Rain cannot walk. ✓ As I was walking home, it started to rain.

After a noun (reduced relative clause): drop who / that and the auxiliary. the people who are waiting outside → the people waiting outside. the houses that were built in 1900 → the houses built in 1900. After the first, the last, the only use to + infinitive: the first person to arrive.

Not and conjunctions. Put not before the participle: Not knowing the way, we asked a stranger. You can keep a conjunction to make the meaning clear: While waiting for the bus, I read a book. After leaving school, she travelled. When asked, he refused.

Typical mistakes: ✗ Walking home, the rain started. → ✓ Walking home, I got wet. (same subject) · ✗ Finish the report, she left. → ✓ Having finished the report, she left. · ✗ the letter writing yesterday → ✓ the letter written yesterday (-ed for passive, -ing only for active)

concept.noteHtml: Participle clauses sound formal. In speech we usually use a full clause: While I was walking home… Use them in writing, and do not stack too many in one sentence. The participle alone as an adjective (a broken window, an interesting book) is in -ed and -ing adjectives. The reduced relative clause comes from relative clauses, and the -ed form is the passive without be (see The passive). Time words like while, after, when are in time clauses. Being is usually left out before an adjective: (Being) tired, she went to bed. Verbs like know and want, which are rare in the continuous, are fine in a participle clause: Not knowing the way, we asked a stranger.

listen.text: The documents requested by the council are missing.
listen.note: -ed, passive: the documents that were requested.

listen.text: Walking home, Amira saw an old friend.
listen.note: -ing, active and at the same time: while she was walking home.

listen.text: Having finished the report, Priya went home.
listen.note: having + -ed: she finished first, then she went home.

hoeren.instruction: Listen and choose the words you hear. Listen for -ing, -ed and having + -ed.

items.text: Having read the email, Kwame replied at once.
The people living next door are very friendly.
Shocked by the news, Olga sat down.
The report published yesterday is online.
Not knowing the way, we asked a stranger.
While waiting for the bus, Amira read a book.

rounds.label: 1 · Relative clause → short phrase
rounds.instruction: You hear a noun with a relative clause. Say it again as a short participle phrase.

example.prompt: the man who is sitting there

items.prompt: the children who are playing in the park
items.answer: the children playing in the park

items.prompt: the report that was published yesterday
the girl who is waiting outside
the houses that were built in 1900
the bus that goes to Leeds
the people who were invited to the party
items.answer: the people invited to the party

rounds.label: 2 · Two sentences → one
rounds.instruction: You hear two short sentences with the same subject. Join them with a participle clause at the start.

example.prompt: I was walking home. I saw Tom.

items.prompt: Amira finished the report. She went home.
items.answer: Having finished the report, Amira went home.

items.prompt: Tom was tired. He went to bed early.
items.answer: Tired, Tom went to bed early.

items.prompt: Liam didn't know the way. He asked a stranger.
items.answer: Not knowing the way, Liam asked a stranger.

items.prompt: Mei was waiting for the bus. She read a book.
items.answer: Waiting for the bus, Mei read a book.

items.prompt: Priya was shocked by the news. She sat down.
items.answer: Shocked by the news, Priya sat down.

items.prompt: Diego had locked the door. He left.
items.answer: Having locked the door, Diego left.

exercises.title: From relative clause to short phrase.
exercises.hint: Drop who / that and the auxiliary. Active (is doing) gives -ing. Passive (was done) gives -ed.

exercises.title: -ing, -ed or having + -ed?
exercises.hint: Same time and active: -ing. Done to the subject: -ed. Finished first: having + -ed. Not: put not before the participle.

exercises.title: Which full sentence matches?
exercises.hint: Tap the participle sentence, then the full-clause version with the same meaning.

exercises.title: Back to a full clause.
exercises.hint: Put back the conjunction or who / that, the subject and the auxiliary. Pick the clause with the same meaning.

exercises.title: Gap text: A local news report.
exercises.hint: Write the participle. The verb and the form are in brackets.
